items.title: More than 99 percent of the visible universe is in a state not taught at GCSE
items.claim: Solid, liquid, gas — the three states of matter on the syllabus. But more than 99 percent of normal matter in the universe (stars, ionised interstellar medium) is plasma — a hot ionised gas with free electrons and ions.
items.prompt: What makes plasma a separate state of matter from a hot gas?

options.text: Plasma is denser than a gas
In plasma the atoms have been ionised so electrons and ions move independently; the substance conducts electricity, responds strongly to electric and magnetic fields, and emits its own light
Plasma is hotter only in name
Plasma is gas that has been compressed

items.reveal:
Heat any gas above a few thousand kelvin and electrons start to break free from atoms. The collection of free electrons and ions is a plasma. Stars, lightning, neon signs, fluorescent lamps and the auroras are all plasmas.

Because charges are free, plasmas have collective behaviours that gases lack: they conduct electricity, they pinch and twist under their own magnetic fields, they support waves that no gas can carry. Magnetohydrodynamics is the whole branch of physics that deals with their flow.

Fusion energy research (ITER, JET, tokamaks) depends on confining hydrogen plasma at over 100 million K with magnetic fields. The plasma cannot touch any wall — the wall would vaporise long before the plasma cooled.
items.why: The 'three states' are good for Earth-surface chemistry. Cosmically, plasma is the default.

items.title: Haber and Bosch fed half the world (and made the explosives that killed millions)
items.claim: In 1909 Fritz Haber at Karlsruhe demonstrated lab-scale ammonia synthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen. By 1913 Carl Bosch at BASF had scaled it to industrial production. The process now feeds about half of humanity through synthetic fertilisers — and the same ammonia was the basis of WWI explosives.
items.prompt: Why is the Haber-Bosch process considered the most consequential industrial chemistry of the 20th century?

options.text: It is the cheapest reaction known

It made cheap nitrogen fertiliser, lifting the cap on global food production and supporting the population growth from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 8 billion today; without it, several billion people could not be fed
It was the first reaction to use a catalyst

items.reveal_title: Two Nobels and a moral weight
items.reveal:
N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3 over an iron catalyst at 400-450°C and 150-300 atm. Single-pass yield is about 15 percent; unreacted gases are recycled to give high throughput.

Haber won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The award was controversial — he had also led Germany's poison gas programme during WWI, personally supervising the first large chlorine gas attack at Ypres in 1915. His first wife Clara Immerwahr, also a chemist, killed herself in protest a week later.

Bosch won the 1931 Nobel Prize for the engineering of high-pressure synthesis. The plant scaled to feed both fertilisers (peace) and explosives (war).

The Haber-Bosch process consumes about 1-2 percent of the world's energy today and accounts for a meaningful fraction of global CO2 emissions. Replacing it with green ammonia (using renewable hydrogen) is a current frontier.
items.why: A single chemical reaction underpins modern population scale. Its history is bound up with both food security and industrial warfare.
